newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK people remember Tiananmen and doubt free future.
newsitem.headline: HK people remember Tiananmen and doubt free future.

text.p: Hong Kong people recalled Beijing's bloody 1989 anti-democracy crackdown on Wednesday, with some voicing doubt that they would still be free to hold Tiananmen vigils after China takes over.
Images of People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops and tanks rolling into Tiananmen Square to crush a student-led democracy movement are still vivid in Hong Kong's collective memory.
The violence in Beijing on June 4, 1989, brought a million people flooding into Hong Kong's streets in anger.
Oliver Ng, an investment bank worker, said public commemorations were unlikely to be permitted after Britain hands the metropolis to China on July 1 after 156 years of colonial rule.
"It is something that will be against the system," Ng said.
Although an annual candlelight vigil, set for Wednesday evening, has become more commemoration than demonstration, emotions still run strong among the territory's 6.4 million people.
Student Cheung Tam-man said the vigil was a time to "just be quiet, sit down and think about what China's government has done".
Despite concerns about civil liberties being watered down after the handover, Cheung said he thought marches would be allowed -- within limits.
"I think it will be okay for demonstrations but not to attack the government," he said.
In street interviews, two other men agreed, saying the June 4 commemoration would probably continue but under certain conditions.
"It really depends on government policy," one said.

Tung Chee-hwa, the former shipping magnate who will lead Hong Kong after the transition to Chinese rule, has pledged lawful demonstrations will be allowed, despite moves by his government-in-waiting to tighten civil liberties.
On Monday, Tung urged Hong Kong people to "put aside the baggage of June 4" to ensure a smooth transition.
One woman said she thought the annual vigils would continue but the significance would fade.
"I don't think it will be as large-scale as before," she said. "As time goes by I think people will forget June 4."
Leung Kwok-hung, a pro-democracy activist and organiser of the vigil, said he was not optimistic about the future.
"I don't think the government will allow the people of Hong Kong to have a demonstration," he told Reuters during a rally on Thursday outside the Chinese mission in the territory.
"They would like to compromise towards some of the big organisations to keep a low profile but they will make an effort to suppress the small groups like us."
